opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it is that we're still quite early. If you look at where the energy has gone over the last few years, it's been overwhelmingly on language. Text is this incredibly dense, compressed representation of human knowledge, and there's an enormous amount of it on the internet, so it was the natural place for scaling to show results first. Images, video, audio, they're richer in some sense, but they're also much less information-dense per bit, and they're more expensive to train on and to run.

But I actually think the impact of multimodality is going to be quite profound, and maybe people are underestimating it a bit. When you have systems that really understand what they're seeing, not just captioning an image but understanding video, understanding physical scenes, understanding diagrams and interfaces, that opens up a huge range of applications that pure text models just can't touch. A lot of the world isn't written down. A lot of what humans do involves looking at things, manipulating things, navigating spaces.

So I think what we've seen so far is the first wave, where multimodal models are kind of bolted-on capabilities. You can show a model a picture and ask a question about it, and that's nice, but it's not yet transformative. The transformative part comes when that understanding becomes grounded and integrated, when the model genuinely builds rich representations of the world from many modalities, and when it can act on that understanding, in robotics, in using computers the way a person does, in science where a lot of the data isn't text at all.

And I think as that happens, people will look back and realize that text-only models were in some ways quite a narrow slice of what intelligence is about. Humans are fundamentally multimodal creatures. So I expect over the next few years multimodality will go from feeling like a nice extra to being central to what these systems can do.

r001.rationale: The response predicts grounded world understanding from integrated multimodal representations and mentions video understanding, but does not say that processing large amounts of video will produce that understanding.

r002.rationale: It says multimodal systems can enable applications pure text models cannot, including robotics, computer use, and science.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there are a few things going on. The first is that language turned out to be an unusually good place to start. Text is compressed, it's abundant, and it already carries a huge amount of structured human knowledge. So when you scale up a language model, you get this very broad competence quite quickly, and that's what people have been experiencing. Images and video are richer in one sense, but they're also much more raw. There's a lot of pixels and not that much semantic content per bit, so you have to work harder to extract something useful.

The second thing is that the obvious applications of multimodality are less immediately compelling to most people. If I can type a question and get a good answer, that's already a very useful product. Being able to also show it a photo is nice, but for most tasks it's an incremental improvement rather than a step change. The places where it becomes really important, I think, are when the system has to act in the world. Robotics, agents that operate a computer screen, understanding a physical environment. Those are domains where you simply can't do the task without perception, and that's where I expect multimodality to matter enormously. But those applications are harder to build, and they're earlier in their development.

And the third is that we're still learning how to train these things well together. It's not obvious how to balance the modalities, how much video you need versus text, how to get real transfer between them rather than just a model that happens to do several things. Some of what you'd hope for, like grounding language in visual experience so the model understands the world more deeply, is starting to appear, but I don't think we've fully realised that promise yet. My expectation is that this shifts quite a lot over the next few years. Video in particular contains an enormous amount of information about how the world works, about physics and causality and everyday behaviour, and once models can really learn from that at scale, I think you'll see the impact become much more visible.

r001.rationale: The response says video contains substantial information about how the world works and predicts that learning from it at scale will make multimodal AI’s impact more visible, alongside deeper grounding.

r002.rationale: It identifies robotics, computer-operating agents, and physical-environment understanding as applications that require perception and go beyond text-only question answering.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that there’s a difference between being able to process different modalities and being able to use them together to do something reliably useful. You can show a system an image and ask questions about it, and that’s impressive. But if you want it to watch what you’re doing, understand your goal, and help you over an extended period of time, you need more than image recognition. You need memory, reasoning, and the ability to keep track of what’s happening.

There’s also a question of where the value is easiest to capture. A lot of economically valuable work already happens in text: writing software, reading documents, answering questions. So language alone gets you quite a long way.

I would expect multimodality to become much more important as these systems move from answering isolated questions to interacting with the world. But I wouldn’t assume that adding another input modality, by itself, produces that change. The rest of the system has to be capable enough to make use of it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions watching a person’s activity and understanding their goal, but it does not predict that processing large amounts of video will give AI a more grounded understanding of the world.

r002.rationale: It says multimodality will matter more as systems move from answering isolated questions to interacting with the world, including helping over an extended period—identifying uses beyond text-only chat.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is that the capabilities are still uneven. A system can look at an image and give you a very impressive description, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can reliably follow what’s happening in a video, understand the causal structure, and then take the right action.

Language also has this enormous advantage: so much of the work we do on computers is already expressed in text. You can get quite a long way just by making a system better at reading and writing. With other modalities, you often need more of the surrounding system to work before the capability becomes useful.

But I wouldn’t conclude that multimodality is somehow less important. If you want an agent that understands the world and can operate in it, it needs to connect what it reads with what it sees and hears. I expect the impact to grow as those capabilities become more reliable and better integrated.

r001.rationale: The response says video understanding and causal reasoning remain unreliable, but does not predict that processing large amounts of video will ground AI systems’ understanding of the world.

r002.rationale: It says an agent that understands and operates in the world needs to connect text with what it sees and hears, identifying multimodality as enabling that broader application.
